abstract: Between-scanner variability in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived features can be comparable to biological between-subject variability, even for the same individual scanned at different sites. MRI harmonisation is therefore an essential tool to ensure studies are generalisable across sites, reducing between-scanner variability and enabling pooling of data to achieve large sample sizes and more representative population samples. Denoising using MPPCA is widely used in preprocessing pipelines for diffusion MRI acquisitions to improve image SNR and it has been proposed as an implicit way of harmonising data. In this registered report, we hypothesised that denoising reduces cross-scanner variability and improves reliability in diffusion MRI metrics without changing cross-scanner bias, and that susceptibility-induced off-resonance reduces its efficacy. We tested these hypotheses using a travelling-heads resource of ten subjects scanned on six scanners from three vendors (GE, Philips, Siemens), with within-scanner repeats. We found that: i) Denoising reduced voxel-wise cross-scanner coefficients of variation for fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and mean kurtosis (MK) (BF > 100; median -3%, -9% and -32%). ROI-wise, variability decreased for MK (-12%), increased for FA (+8%), and evidence was inconclusive for MD. ii) Contrary to our hypothesis, denoising changed cross-scanner bias in every subject-scanner pair, by up to 3% of the mean; in exploratory analyses, this change was strongly related to contrast-to-noise ratio. iii) Evidence for a change in the registered measure of reliability was inconclusive, although exploratory analyses showed higher voxel-wise reliability after denoising. iv) There was no convincing evidence that off-resonance reduces denoising efficacy. Together, these results suggest that MPPCA denoising reduces the random, noise-driven component of cross-scanner variability, most strongly at the voxel level and for kurtosis, but does not consistently reduce systematic differences between scanners. As such, it should complement harmonisation, not replace it.
